title: Leaving Punjab
hookLine: from the late 1800s Sikhs went as soldiers, police and workers to Malaya, Hong Kong and East Africa

cards: Old photographs of Hong Kong, from about a hundred years ago, show tall policemen in turbans directing traffic. In Singapore and Malaya, the same: Sikh police and watchmen.
In Kenya and Uganda, Punjabi workers laid the railway line through the bush toward Lake Victoria. How did a farming people from one corner of India end up across Asia and Africa?
And far from any gurdwara, what did they bring with them?

teach.b: After the British took Punjab in 1849, they began recruiting Sikhs into their army in great numbers, and Sikhs served across the empire. But the empire needed more than soldiers.
It needed police for its port cities, guards for its banks and docks, and workers for its railways.

So from the late 1800s, young Punjabi men, many of them Sikh, went out: as police to Hong Kong and Shanghai, as police and watchmen to Singapore and the Malay states, and as builders and craftsmen to East Africa, where tens of thousands of workers from India laid the Uganda Railway.
Most went to earn and send money home. Many meant to return. Some did.
Others stayed, married, and built lives.
The Punjabi word for this is pardes, a foreign land, and pardesi, one who is far from home. There are Punjabi folk songs full of longing for the pardesi who went away.
And wherever a few Sikhs gathered, they did something simple.

teach.h: A ROOM, THE GURU, A SANGAT.
teach.b: They set aside a room, installed the Guru Granth Sahib with respect, and began to sing. A corner of a police barracks, a rented room, later a proper building. That is all a gurdwara needs: the Guru, and a sangat.
So some of the earliest gurdwaras abroad rose in these places, around the start of the twentieth century. The Sikhs who left Punjab did not leave the Guru behind.
They carried the Guru with them, with respect, and made a new home wherever the Guru rested.

how: Wherever Sikhs settle, they install the Guru Granth Sahib in a room or building and gather for kirtan and langar; many of the oldest gurdwaras abroad began this way in Asia and East Africa.

games.q: you're a young Sikh policeman in a port city far from Punjab, with a few other Sikhs and no gurdwara. what do you do?
o: wait until you're home to go to a gurdwara.
set aside a room, install the Guru, and begin to sing.
give up the practice until you return.
games.why: that's how the first gurdwaras abroad began: a room, the Guru Granth Sahib, and a sangat.

practice: Bring to mind one person who left home to earn a living: a parent, a grandparent, a colleague, the person who cleans your office or delivers your food.
Picture the place they miss and the people they send money to, and wonder what they carried with them that you can't see: a faith, a song, a way of cooking. Hold them warmly.

wordCard.voice: Leaving Punjab. From the late 1800s, Sikhs went out as soldiers, police and workers to Malaya, Hong Kong and East Africa, and took the Guru with them.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pardes, a foreign land; a pardesi is one far from home, a figure of many Punjabi songs.

carryVoice: Your line: carrying the guru abroad. A rented room could become a gurdwara. See you tomorrow.
